questions.q: What happens to precision and recall when you lower the classification cutoff from 0.5 to 0.15?
options: Recall rises and precision usually falls, because more customers are flagged
questions.explain: A lower cutoff flags more customers. You catch more real positives (higher recall) but more flagged customers are false alarms (lower precision).

questions.q: Why does the lesson use cross_val_predict on the training set to choose the cutoff?
options: It gives honest probabilities for training rows, so the test set stays untouched for a final confirmation
questions.explain: Each row's probability comes from a model that did not see that row. That lets you tune the cutoff without using the test set, which would otherwise stop being an honest estimate.

questions.q: A missed churner costs $100 and a false alarm costs $20. Compared with the default 0.5, where should the cost-minimizing cutoff be expected to fall?
options: Higher than 0.5, since misses are cheap
Lower than 0.5, since misses cost more than false alarms
It does not depend on the costs
questions.explain: When false negatives are more expensive, it pays to flag more customers, which means a lower cutoff. In the lesson it was 0.15.

questions.q: Why compare the tuned model against 'flag everyone' and 'flag nobody' strategies?
options: To check that the model adds value beyond trivial policies under the same costs
questions.explain: Flagging everyone cost 3,820 and flagging nobody cost 5,900, while the tuned cutoff cost 2,860. Beating both shows the model genuinely helps under these costs.

questions.q: In confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred).ravel() for a binary problem, what is the order of the four returned counts?
questions.explain: Rows are actual classes and columns are predicted classes, so flattening gives true negatives, false positives, false negatives, then true positives.
